# elements.py
*`src/pySEA/rayTEM/elements.py`*

## Overview

`elements.py` defines the ray convention, the column utility functions, and all concrete element types used in ray-tracing simulations. Every optic — lenses, drifts, apertures, dipoles, quadrupoles, prisms — is an `Element` subclass that implements a `transfer_matrix()` (ray side) and a `phase_shift()` (wave side). The base class `propagate_ray()` applies the matrix via `einsum` and additively updates z and the affine shift/tilt terms. This module is the foundation: everything in `assemblies.py` depends on it.

**Ray column convention** (6 purely geometric columns, index 0–5):

| Index | Name | Meaning |
|-------|------|---------|
| 0 | `x` | lateral position in x |
| 1 | `xt` | angle in x (xθ) |
| 2 | `y` | lateral position in y |
| 3 | `yt` | angle in y (yθ) |
| 4 | `z` | position along the optical axis |
| 5 | `E` | electron energy (keV; 0 when `Source.voltage` unset) |

The column ordering is frozen — `columnByName()` is the only safe way to access a column by name. Never hard-code column indices.

**Intensity (I) and cumulative Larmor rotation (R) are NOT ray columns.** They
travel as separate parallel `(n_planes, n_rays)` arrays on
`MicroscopeSection`/`Microscope` (`.I`/`.R`), updated per element via
`Element.apply_intensity` (before `propagate_ray` — e.g. `Aperture` attenuates
by the cropped-area fraction) and `Element.apply_rotation` (after — thick
lenses accumulate `self.rotation`). Any code reading `columnByName("I")`/`("R")`
is stale.

---

## Module-level functions

### `columnByName(name)`

Returns the integer index of the named column in the `convention` list. The one safe way to index rays by column: `rays[:, columnByName("x")]`. Using this instead of raw integers means column reordering won't silently corrupt element code.

### `fix_mat_dims(m, columnNames)`

Inflates a smaller physics matrix (e.g. a 2×2 thin-lens matrix operating on [x, xt]) into the full 6×6 convention matrix (sized off `len(convention)`). Off-diagonal entries for unspecified columns remain zero; diagonal entries remain 1 (identity). Every element's `transfer_matrix()` should call this before returning.

### `fix_ray_dims(rays, columnNames)`

Same idea as `fix_mat_dims` but for ray arrays. Given a compact `(N, k)` array whose columns correspond to `columnNames`, returns a full `(N, 6)` array in convention order, with unspecified columns zero. Used by `Source.rays()` to build the initial ray set.

---

## Element

Base class for all optic elements. It is **transparent by default in every propagation kind** — identity transfer matrix (rays/moments), a phase of nothing plus free transport over its `length` (waves) — so any element propagates out of the box and subclasses override only what their physics requires.

### `Element.__init__(self, name, kind)`

Stores `name` and `kind`, and seeds the transparent default `length = 0`. Concrete element subclasses call `super().__init__()` and then set their physics attributes (`strength`, `length`, `position`, `calibration`, etc.).

### `Element.transfer_matrix(self)`

Returns a 6×6 numpy array. The base class returns the **identity** (a transparent element); subclasses with ray physics override it, building the matrix with `fix_mat_dims`.

### `Element.propagate_ray(self, r0, z, z0)`

Applies `transfer_matrix()` to the input ray array via `einsum('mn,in->im', M, r0)`, then additively applies `self.length` to the `z` column and any affine `shift_x`/`shift_y`/`tilt_x`/`tilt_y` terms. These updates are additive, not part of the matrix — this keeps the matrix physics clean. Rotation is NOT applied here: the drivers call `apply_rotation` separately (R is a parallel array, not a ray column). Returns `(N, 6)` ray array.

`Dipole` overrides this because it uses an augmented (affine) matrix form.

### `Element.phase_shift(self, dimensions, wavelength, scaled=False, s=1.0)`

The wave-side element contract (counterpart of `transfer_matrix`): each element
class **states its wave physics explicitly** — nothing is derived from the ray
matrix. `scaled=False` returns the ordered phase program for the fixed-grid
propagator: a list of space-tagged phase Signals (`space='position'` = real
screen, `space='scattering'` = reciprocal free-segment kernel); finite length
yields `[kernel(L/2), screen, kernel(L/2)]` via `_phase_program`. `scaled=True`
returns the split `(power, screen)`: `power` is absorbed into the curvature
state (Eq 45) and `screen` is the non-absorbable phase applied explicitly to U
at physical coords x = s·ξ (Eqs 47–48; `None` when fully absorbed).
Definitions: Lens χ = −k(x²+y²)/2f (scaled: full 1/f → R, no screen);
Quadrapole χ = −k(x²−y²)/2f_q saddle (scaled: per-axis powers ((P_x, P_y),
None) absorbed into the **anisotropic** curvature (R_x, R_y) — no screen, no
sampling limit, arbitrarily strong stigmators run);
Dipole χ = k(θ_x·x + θ_y·y) (scaled: full screen, evaluated at per-axis
physical pitch s_x·dξ / s_y·dη on anisotropic frames); Drift reciprocal kernel
(scaled: `(0.0, None)` — the driver runs the free segment). The base `Element`
is **transparent** (the wave analog of the identity matrix): a phase of
nothing plus free transport over its `length` — fixed path returns a single
full-length kernel (empty program at zero length), scaled path returns
`(0.0, None)`. Source/Aperture/Prism override it to fail loudly because their
wave action is not a phase.

### `Element.scaled_segment(self)`
Lets an element declare itself a **segment** rather than a point event for the
scaled wave path. Base `Element` returns `None` ("treat me as a kick and/or
screen inside free space"); `Lens.scaled_segment` returns `('quadratic', K)`
when `length > 0` and `K != 0`, because a thick round lens is a
quadratic-index medium the frame can follow exactly (sinusoidal `s(z)`,
closed-form Δτ, no screen). `length == 0` returns `None`, so a thin lens keeps
the curvature-kick route through `phase_shift(scaled=True)` bit-for-bit. Only
the scaled/hybrid paths consult this — a fixed grid cannot follow the
medium's scale law, so the fixed path still slices thick elements.

### `Element.propagate_wave(self, signal, mode='fixed', s_min=1e-3, log=None, absorb=0.1, crossover='flat', rotate=False)`

The one wave method covering all three representations via `mode`:

- `'fixed'` — fixed-grid propagation: consumes `phase_shift(scaled=False)` and
  applies each item with `waveoptics.apply_phase`.
- `'scaled'` — scaled-Fresnel on a single frame (handoff Eqs 23–48): state is
  a scaled wavefield Signal (U on ξ/η Dimensions + s/R/τ/z/λ metadata). Free
  L/2 → `phase_shift(scaled=True)` consumption (power →
  `apply_thin_lens_scaled`; screen → sampling guard, per-pixel |Δχ| < π, then
  applied to U) → free L/2. Raises before a beam crossover (the frame's s = 0
  singularity).
- `'hybrid'` — the scaled representation with automatic frame switching: free
  segments run through `waveoptics.propagate_free_scaled_hybrid`, which
  flattens converging frames before their crossover, logs the crossover
  (back-focal) plane, and re-diverges past it. Interior planes are appended to
  the optional `log` list as tagged scaled Signals.

A thick lens (`length > 0`) is routed through
`waveoptics.propagate_thick_lens_scaled` as one exact segment instead of
*drift L/2 → kick → drift L/2*; this is what brought the hybrid crossovers
onto the ray-traced diffraction planes (they previously sat 422–4808 µm away
on `basic_column`). `rotate=True` additionally applies each thick lens's
Larmor rotation `−K·L` to the wave, matching the ray path (off by default —
a no-op for rotationally symmetric fields).

`absorb` is the absorbing-boundary margin for the free segments (default 0.1;
0 disables — pure periodic FFT); `crossover` picks the hybrid traversal policy
(`'flat'` default, `'jump'` for direct mirror frame jumps — see the waveoptics
wiki for the measured guidance). Frame state is scalar-or-pair throughout: a
quadrupole makes the frame anisotropic (per-axis s/R/τ, line-focus events
tagged `flatten-x`/`crossover-y`/…), while round-lens columns stay scalar
bit-for-bit. Internally split into `_propagate_wave_fixed` /
`_propagate_wave_scaled`. Larmor rotation is not applied to the wavefield
(documented approximation).

### `Element.propagate(self, *args, kind='ray', **kwargs)`

Unified dispatcher: `kind` ∈ ray/rays, moments/envelope/covariance, wave,
wave-scaled/wave_scaled, wave-hybrid/wave_hybrid → `_PROPAGATE_KINDS` maps to
`(method, forced kwargs)` — the wave kinds all route to the one
`propagate_wave` with the matching `mode`.

## Source

A pseudo-element that generates the initial ray set. Placed first in a `MicroscopeSection`; when `propagate_ray` encounters a `Source` as the first element and no `r0` is provided, it calls `Source.rays()` to produce the starting rays.

### `Source.__init__(self, name, size, np_xy, angle, na_xy, position)`

- `size` — (x_half, y_half) extent of the emission grid
- `np_xy` — (nx, ny) number of grid points
- `angle` — (xt_max, yt_max) half-angle range
- `na_xy` — (nxt, nyt) number of angle steps

### `Source.rays(self)`

Constructs a full 2D grid of (position × angle) rays via `meshgrid`-style broadcasting. Returns shape `(np_xy[0] × np_xy[1] × na_xy[0] × na_xy[1], 6)`; the `E` column is filled with `voltage` when set. Intensity is not a ray column — the section/microscope drivers seed the separate `.I` array with ones.

### `Source.propagate_ray(self, r0, **kwargs)`

No-op: passes `r0` through unchanged. Exists so `MicroscopeSection.propagate_ray` can iterate over all elements including the Source without special-casing it.

### `Source.wave(self, mode='fixed')` / `Source._aperture_wave(self, radius)`

The source holds **one wavefunction generator**: `wave(mode=...)` builds the
initial wave on the source's grid (`wave_shape`/`wave_extent`, wavelength from
`voltage`) of the kind selected by `wave_kind` —
`'plane' | 'gaussian' | 'point' | 'aperture'`, where `'aperture'` is the
flat-intensity hard-aperture wave Θ(a−r) at `aperture_radius` (handoff Eq 9,
implemented by the `_aperture_wave(radius)` builder). `mode='fixed'` returns
the physical wavefield Signal; `'scaled'`/`'hybrid'` seed the scaled state
with s = 1, R = ∞, τ = 0 so U₀ = ψ₀ (Eqs 10–11). `Source.propagate_wave` is a
passthrough in every mode (drivers seed from the generator).

---

## Aperture

Models a circular aperture by scaling down rays proportionally when the beam exceeds the aperture radius. Does not zero out rays (to keep the fitting landscape smooth); instead rescales all x and y coordinates so the outermost ray just touches the edge, and reduces I by the area ratio.

### `Aperture.__init__(self, name, radius, calibration, position)`

`calibration` is an optional linear scale on `radius` (e.g. the physical aperture is 2 mm but measured to be 1.95 mm).

### `Aperture.propagate_ray(self, r0, z, z0)`

Finds `xmax = max(|x|)` and `ymax = max(|y|)` across all rays. If either exceeds `self.radius`, scales all x, xt, y, yt by `radius/xmax` or `radius/ymax` respectively (`_aperture_scales`). Intensity is reduced separately: `Aperture.apply_intensity` multiplies the parallel `I` array by the product of both scale factors (area reduction). The aperture has no `transfer_matrix` — it overrides `propagate_ray` entirely.

### `Aperture.propagate_wave(self, signal, mode='fixed', ...)`

One mode-aware override: an aperture is an amplitude mask, not a phase
(`phase_shift` raises). `mode='fixed'` zeros the field outside `radius`
(`waveoptics.aperture_mask`); `'scaled'`/`'hybrid'` mask U at the scaled
radius `radius/|s|` (physical r ≤ radius ⇔ ξ ≤ radius/|s|), frame state and
crossover marker unchanged.

---

## Drift

Free-space propagation: `x₂ = x₁ + xt₁ * L`, `y₂ = y₁ + yt₁ * L`. Named drifts serve as fiducial planes (e.g. "sample" or "CCD") that appear as vertical lines in `plot2D`.

### `Drift.__init__(self, name, length, calibration, position)`

`calibration` is an optional linear scale on `length`, useful when fitted lens positions differ from the nominal schematic positions.

### `Drift.transfer_matrix(self)`

Returns an 8×8 matrix with `m[x, xt] = L` and `m[y, yt] = L` (i.e. `x_new = x + xt*L`). If `calibration` is set, `L = length * calibration`.

---

## Quadrapole

Asymmetric focusing element: focuses in x while defocusing in y (or vice versa). Used in aberration-corrected columns and steering systems.

### `Quadrapole.__init__(self, name, position, length, strength, calibration)`

`kind` is set to `'Thin quad'` if `length == 0`, else `'Quad'`. `calibration` can be a scalar (linear) or `(scale, power)` tuple for power-law scaling of strength.

### `Quadrapole.transfer_matrix(self)`

For thin quads (length=0) uses the thin-lens approximation matrix directly. For thick quads (length>0) uses the cos/sin solution to the Hill equation (Brown 1983 p. 46): the x and y 2×2 matrices differ in the sign of the quadrupole term, producing focusing in one plane and defocusing in the other. Both 2×2 matrices are assembled separately via `fix_mat_dims` then matrix-multiplied.

---

## Dipole

Steering element that applies a constant angular kick in x, y, or an arbitrary transverse direction. The steering term is affine (constant kick independent of ray position), so Dipole uses an augmented (7×8) matrix instead of the standard square form.

### `Dipole.__init__(self, name, position, length, strength, calibration, axis)`

`axis` controls the kick direction: `'x'` or `'y'` as strings, a float in radians, or a `[x, y]` sequence. Internally stored as `phi` (radians from x-axis). `kind` is `'Thin dipole'` or `'Dipole'`.

### `Dipole.transfer_matrix(self)`

Returns a `(7, 8)` augmented matrix where the 8th column carries the affine terms (constant kick). For a thin dipole: angular kicks in x and y go into `m[xt, 8]` and `m[yt, 8]`. For a thick dipole: adds drift terms and quadratic position offsets (`0.5*K*L²`). The matrix is not square, so Dipole cannot use `Element.propagate_ray`.

### `Dipole.propagate_ray(self, r0, z, z0)`

Overrides the base class. Appends a column of ones to `r0` to form `r0_aug` `(N, 8)`, then applies the `(7, 8)` matrix via einsum. The "ones" column makes the affine kick additive when multiplied.

---

## Lens

Round (symmetric) magnetic lens. The dominant optic in TEM columns. A thick lens additionally rotates the beam by angle `K*L` radians (Larmor rotation) — this is tracked in the `R` column via `Element.propagate_ray`.

### `Lens.__init__(self, name, length, strength, calibration, position)`

`kind` is `'Thin lens'` if `length == 0`, else `'QLens'`. `strength` is proportional to lens current; `strength²` is proportional to `1/f`. `calibration` can be:
- a scalar `c`: `K = strength * c`
- a list `[A, B, C, ...]`: `K = A + B*strength^(1/1) + C*strength^(1/2) + D*strength^(1/3) + ...`

The polynomial-root form lets calibration curves be fitted from experimental data.

### `Lens.transfer_matrix(self)`

Three cases:
1. `K == 0`: acts as a Drift (thin or thick).
2. `length == 0` (thin lens): 4×4 matrix with `-K²` on the off-diagonal position→angle entries, identical for x and y.
3. `length > 0` (thick lens, Brown 1983 p. 106): uses the cos/sin form `[[C, iK*S], [-KS, C]]` for both x and y independently. Sets `self.rotation = -K*L`; `propagate_ray` will add this to the R column.

### `Lens.calibration_from_f_and_I(self, f, I, rotationPerAmp)`

Computes `self.calibration` from a known focal length `f` and excitation current `I`. Uses `scipy.minimize` to solve the nonlinear equation `K*sin(K*L)*cos(K*L) = 1/f`. If `rotationPerAmp` is also provided, simultaneously fits `self.length`.

---

## Prism

Magnetic sector / energy spectrometer element. Models EELS-type spectrometers: entrance/exit focusing at the pole-face edges plus the bending field in between. Work in progress — dispersion (R16) and higher-order aberrations are listed as TODOs.

### `Prism.__init__(self, name, position, length, radius, angle, w, g, k1, strength, calibration)`

Either `length` or `radius` must be provided (not both). The other is derived from `length = angle_rad * radius`. `w` and `g` are fringe-field parameters; `k1` enables fringe-field edge focusing.

### `Prism.focus_matrix(self)`

Returns the 8×8 transfer matrix for the entrance or exit pole-face. When `K1 != 0` includes fringe-field correction via `psi`.

### `Prism.bending_matrix(self, s)`

Returns the 8×8 transfer matrix for the arc-length `s` inside the bending magnet. Uses cos/sin of `s/radius` for the dispersive plane.

### `Prism.transfer_matrix(self)`

Composes `focus_matrix @ bending_matrix @ focus_matrix` to get the full spectrometer matrix.
